profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a proprietary trading firm, Meridian Peak Capital, after the intraday equity-index risk monitor began producing repeated false volatility alerts during heavy market activity around scheduled macro announcements. The monitor feeds into automated position throttles for the firm's E-mini S&P 500 futures strategies, and on the last three CPI/FOMC days it cut trading more aggressively than expected despite no corresponding spike in realized post-event losses. The meeting is between the head of intraday risk analytics and the market data/platform lead to diagnose why the model is overreacting. The agenda is to compare what changed in the alert pipeline, determine whether the issue comes from the return model, the trade-arrival inputs, or event handling, and agree on a fix that can be deployed before next week's payrolls release. The expected outcome is a shared action plan for a 'stability patch' to the volatility monitor and a concrete definition of what evidence will count as the issue being fixed.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: High-frequency risk modeling, volatility estimation, event-day controls, futures market microstructure
members.background: Elena has a PhD in financial econometrics and spent six years building intraday risk systems for listed derivatives desks before joining Meridian Peak to lead model governance for automated limits and throttles.
members.private_state: She wants a narrowly targeted patch that restores confidence in the existing volatility monitor before payrolls Friday, avoids opening a model re-approval process, and preserves the team's narrative that the underlying return model is sound outside special event windows.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the model should be stable, they mean the alert rate outside explicitly excluded scheduled-news windows should return to its pre-upgrade baseline.
The problematic behavior is most likely a contamination issue around event controls rather than a flaw in the trade-time Gaussian layer.
The 'open' session for this monitor effectively starts at 9:30 a.m. New York because that is when the downstream equity-index risk dashboard is benchmarked.
A hotfix can be implemented by adjusting the preprocessing and event-window exclusions without changing the core model specification or revalidating the arrival process from scratch.

members.name: Marcus Bell
members.role: Director of Market Data & Execution Platform
members.expertise: Feed normalization, timestamping, exchange connectivity, latency diagnostics, real-time pipeline operations
members.background: Marcus came from an exchange infrastructure vendor and now oversees Meridian Peak's normalized futures trade feed, clock synchronization, and the production services that compute real-time features used by execution and risk systems.
members.private_state: He wants to show the production data pipeline is fundamentally healthy, avoid a rushed rollback of last month's feed-normalization upgrade, and contain the fix to operational settings rather than reopening questions about timestamp granularity or architecture.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the model should be stable, they mean the platform should stop generating operationally disruptive throttle events during the full Globex trading day, including overnight.
The issue is probably how the risk service computes trade-arrival bursts from normalized feed events rather than anything about scheduled-news controls.
For E-mini futures, 'the open' naturally refers to the Sunday/overnight Globex session continuity and not specifically the 9:30 a.m. cash-equity open.
A safe patch means changing how bursts are aggregated in the live service while leaving the feed-normalization release intact.
The team already accepts that all event timestamps are handled in exchange/Central Time internally, so no one needs to restate timezone assumptions.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'exclude the news window' when evaluating or patching the false alerts.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means the full control window used in model validation: from 2 minutes before to 10 minutes after pre-scheduled macro releases, plus the first minute after the cash-equity open when an event coincides with it.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means the narrow operational suppression already in production: roughly 30 seconds before to 90 seconds after the exchange-stamped release time, with no special extension tied to the cash-equity open.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both treat 'news window' as an established internal term and assume the other is referring to the same long-standing event-handling convention, so the phrase feels too routine to unpack in a troubleshooting meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to behavior 'around the open' as a key diagnostic period.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena is thinking of the 9:30 a.m. New York cash-equity open because that is where the risk dashboard's baseline comparisons are anchored.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus is thinking of the futures session open/overnight Globex continuity, especially the 8:30 a.m. CT to 9:00 a.m. CT burst patterns that dominate infrastructure load.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In equity-index futures conversations, 'the open' is commonly used without qualification, and each person's role makes their own reference point feel self-evident enough that neither expects ambiguity.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need a patch that 'stabilizes the monitor before payrolls.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena believes the issue is fixed if the monitor's alert frequency and realized-volatility fit return to pre-upgrade behavior on backtests excluding controlled event windows, even if some alerts still occur in live trading.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus believes the issue is fixed if the live system stops triggering repeated throttle cascades on high-traffic mornings, even if the statistical fit to historical baseline distributions is not fully restored.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'stabilize the monitor' sounds naturally shared in a troubleshooting context, and each person assumes the other's criterion is just an operational restatement of their own preferred evidence.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'rebuild the arrival series from raw trades' to check whether the trade-rate input is the source of the problem.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means reconstructing inter-trade durations from economically meaningful trade prints after deduplicating same-timestamp updates and collapsing split fills into a single market event for the model's trade-time process.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means replaying the normalized production feed exactly as consumed by the service, preserving each message-level trade print after exchange sequencing because that is what the live system actually sees.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sincerely think 'raw trades' is the most literal and neutral way to describe the source data, but one is using a modeling notion of raw economic trades while the other is using an engineering notion of raw production messages.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this tightly scoped. The recent CPI and FOMC mornings clearly shook confidence, but I do not want this turning into a wholesale challenge to the return model or a re-approval exercise before payrolls. If we can show the alert rate outside the controlled validation windows goes back to the old baseline, that is enough to stabilize the monitor before payrolls. My bet is still that the issue sits in event handling and preprocessing, not in the Gaussian trade-time layer itself.

turns.inner_thought: I need to make clear the production platform is not broken. Ops didn't see feed drops, clock drift, or sequencing faults. If we can stop the throttle cascades in live conditions without touching the normalization release, that's the safest route.
